paper.title: Spatial wage differentials, geographic frictions and the organization of labor within firms
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability statement (p. 15): 'The authors do not have permission to share data.' Supplementary material related to the article is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.regsciurbeco.2025.104128. …

registers.name_in_paper: Integrated Database for Labor Market Research (IDA)
registers.role: sample frame; treatment and outcomes: establishment-firm-worker matches, hourly wage, tenure, labor market experience, occupation/position, establishment municipality and traffic zone, commuting flows
linkage: firm-level records matched to establishment records
linkage / treatment construction: municipality reported by the firm in its accounting records, used to classify the HQ establishment
treatment/outcome construction: occupation codes used to classify managers

registers.name_in_paper: Population statistics: FAIN register up to 2006

registers.role: instrument construction: immigration status and date of immigration
controls: educational attainment, used in the quality-adjusted wage regression (Eq. (1))

linkages: Employees linked to their job (establishment and firm) via IDA, keeping the match with the most hours in the last week of November
Establishments linked to firms via unique firm and establishment identifiers in IDA, matched to General Firm Statistics (FIRM) and Firm Accounting Statistics (FIRE)

HQ assigned by matching the establishment's municipality to the municipality reported by the firm in its accounting records, conditional on employing at least five workers; residual 4% assigned by concentration of managers, high-wage earners and degree holders
Non-HQ establishments paired with their firm's HQ; when a firm has more than two establishments, the firm's largest non-HQ establishment is used
Workers linked to Population (FAIN/BEF), Immigration (IEPE) and Education (UDDA) registers for age, immigration status and educational attainment
Commuting flows between municipalities computed by year and occupation from the matched employer-employee data (municipality of residence to workplace municipality)
Pre- and post-2007 municipalities linked by an author-constructed crosswalk; Copenhagen and Frederiksberg treated as a single municipality
Establishments located in traffic zones (907 units from the Technical University of Denmark's National Transport Model); distance between establishments measured between traffic-zone centroids

sample.universe: The full population of employers and employees collected by Statistics Denmark (DST) between 1981 and 2016, restricted to firms in manufacturing, transportation, business services, and finance, insurance and real estate (FIRE), which together account for approximately 53% of national employment in Denmark
sample.unit_of_observation: establishment-year (with non-HQ establishments paired to their firm's HQ in the across-establishment specifications)
selection_rules: Keep firms in manufacturing, transportation, business services, and finance, insurance and real estate (FIRE)

Drop establishments with no reported location; those located in sparsely populated islands; establishments with 1 or 2 employees or that only appear one year; firms with more than 99 establishments or with large jumps in the number of establishments across years (sampling criteria follow Acosta and Lyngemark, 2021)
Restrict to individuals between 15 and 80 years old
Keep only each individual's main job (the job with the most normal hours; ties broken by higher wage)
Keep only workers with hourly wages between 50 and 5,500 DKK (restricting the bottom 0.1% and the top 0.01% tails)
Drop observations whose reported wage has strong measurement error (IDA variable TLONKVAL equal to zero or higher than 100, available until 2008)
Drop firms with less than 3 workers, or that had 1 to 3 workers for at least 66% of the sample period
Drop establishments for which no manager could be identified (around one third of establishments, holding around one sixth of the workforce)
Use data from 1996 onward for descriptive statistics and estimations (1986-1994 is reserved as the instrument's base period)
sample.period: 1996-2016 for descriptive statistics and estimation; 1986-1994 base period for the instrument; underlying registers 1981-2016
sample.n_observations: approximately 227k firm-year, 270k establishment-year, and almost 12 million worker-year observations for 1996-2016; estimation samples of 250,774 establishment-year observations (all establishments), 39,162 (non-HQ establishments of multi-establishment firms) and 29,104 (structural estimation)
sample.n_individuals: on average 10,802 firms and 12,865 establishments each year, containing around 562,501 workers

construction_notes: Quality-adjusted establishment-occupation-year wages: log of the raw hourly wage of worker p of occupation c (manager or non-manager, estimated separately) regressed on worker characteristics (gender, region of origin, education interacted with a degree-two polynomial of experience and tenure, detailed occupation and job position dummies) plus establishment-year fixed effects (Eq. (1)); the exponential of the predicted establishment-year fixed effect is the establishment-level wage measure
Efficiency units of labor: M^E_ijt = sum over managers p of exp(X_pmt * beta_m) and L^E_ijt = sum over workers p of exp(X_plt * beta_l), using the estimated coefficients from Eq. (1)
Wages deflated using the 2015 national Consumer Price Index
Manager = categorized as a manager or top executive by either PSTILL/PSOC (IDA) or DISCO88 (AKM); mostly two-digit occupations are used, with a crosswalk for the 2009/2010 DISCO88-to-DISCO08 change
Managers in HQ services defined as those categorized as 'Directors and Chief Executives'; managers in final-good production at the HQ defined as the residual
HQ = establishment whose municipality matches the municipality in the firm's accounting records and that employs at least five workers (identifies an HQ for 96% of firms)
Distance between establishment and HQ = distance between the centroids of their traffic zones
Commuting areas defined by Nielsen (2005) from 2004 commuting flows, averaging 4 municipalities

Immigration share-shifter IS^R_ojt built with base-year occupation-country-municipality shares and the log national stock of immigrants of that occupation and country, leaving municipality j out (Eq. (18)); mapped to workplace municipalities with occupation-specific historical native commuting shares (Eq. (19))
Base period for the instrument's shares and commuting flows: 1986-1994, when Denmark's quasi-random refugee dispersal policy was at full strength
Communication costs assumed to be tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t), with a time-varying distance elasticity c_t
Cost shares gamma_i and omega_h recovered from observed establishment employment and wages and entered at their lagged value

Estimation uses the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem with the method of alternating projections for establishment and year fixed effects (Correia, 2018); variables then demeaned within each sector-commuting-area pair

claims.statement: A positive commuting-augmented immigration shock for managers in the establishment's municipality is associated with a higher quality-adjusted manager wage at the establishment.

treatment.label: 𝐼𝑆𝐹 𝑀𝑗 — commuting-augmented immigration shock for managers in the establishment's workplace municipality j

register_source.value: Population registers FAIN (to 2006) / BEF (from 2007) and IEPE (immigration date) for immigrant stocks by country of origin and municipality; IDA for occupation and for municipality-of-residence-to-workplace commuting flows

definition.value: Shift-share labor supply shock. The residential shock IS^R_ojt = sum_c (L_ocjt0/L_oct0) * log Imm_{o,c,DK-j,t} (Eq. (18)) uses base-year (1986-1994) shares of occupation-o workers from country c living in municipality j and the log national stock of such immigrants leaving municipality j out; it is then mapped to workplace municipality k with occupation-specific historical native commuting shares, IS^F_okt = sum_j IS^R_ojt * pi^D_ojk,t0 (Eq. (19)). Entered in first differences.

outcome.label: log 𝑣𝑖 — log quality-adjusted wage of managers at establishment i

register_source.value: IDA: hourly wage (quality-adjusted establishment-occupation-year wage, estimated as the exponential of the establishment-year fixed effect of Eq. (1))

definition.value: Log of the establishment-level quality-adjusted wage of managers, i.e. the exponential of the establishment-year fixed effect from the Mincer-type regression Eq. (1) estimated on managers only; deflated with the 2015 national CPI. Estimated in first differences.

units.value: log points of the establishment-level quality-adjusted wage per unit of the commuting-augmented immigration share-shifter (the shifter's units are those of Eqs. (18)-(19) and are not reported)

estimand.target_population: All establishments in the estimation sample
estimand.time_horizon: Contemporaneous: the specification is in annual first differences, so the coefficient relates the change in the regressor to the change in the outcome within the same year (1996-2016)

population.description: All establishments in the estimation sample: single-establishment firms plus HQ and non-HQ establishments of multi-establishment firms, 1996-2016 (250,774 establishment-year observations)
population.selection: Firms in manufacturing, transportation, business services and finance, insurance and real estate; establishments with a reported location, outside sparsely populated islands, with more than 2 employees and appearing in more than one year; firms with at least 3 workers and fewer than 100 establishments; workers aged 15-80 with hourly wages between 50 and 5,500 DKK and no flagged wage measurement error; establishments for which at least one manager could be identified (about one third of establishments dropped).

identification.source_of_variation: Commuting-augmented immigration share-shifter: pre-1994 occupation-country-municipality immigrant enclave shares combined with the log national stock of immigrants of that occupation and origin (leaving the municipality out), mapped from municipalities of residence into workplace municipalities with occupation-specific historical native commuting flows (Eqs. (18)-(19)).
identification.instrument: 𝐼𝑆𝐹 𝑀𝑗 — commuting-augmented immigration shock for managers in the establishment's workplace municipality j

key_assumptions.assumption: Shock exogeneity: given establishment and year fixed effects and sector*commuting-area pre-trends, predicted immigration flows are not correlated with unobserved factors driving changes in firms' labor demand decisions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from four features of the Danish setting (rising immigrant employment share since 1994; variation across immigrants' countries of origin and arrival time; EU accession dates; the 1986-1998 quasi-random refugee dispersal policy) and from first-stage robustness in Table A4.

lhs: 𝐼𝑆𝐹 𝑀𝑗 — commuting-augmented immigration shock for managers in the establishment's workplace municipality j
rhs: Unobserved time-varying determinants of the establishment's relative labor demand

population.selection: Firms in manufacturing, transportation, business services and finance, insurance and real estate; establishments with a reported location, outside sparsely populated islands, with more than 2 employees and appearing in more than one year; firms with at least 3 workers and fewer than 100 establishments; workers aged 15-80 with hourly wages between 50 and 5,500 DKK and no flagged wage measurement error; establishments for which at least one manager could be identified (about one third of establishments dropped). claims.statement: Production workers' output elasticity in the establishment's Cobb-Douglas final-good technology is 0.652 in the head-count specification. (Table 5, column (1): the standard specification with all labor quantities measured in head counts.)

treatment.label: 𝐿𝑖 — production workers used as an input in the establishment's final-good production function

register_source.value: IDA: PSTILL/PSOC (job position) and AKM: DISCO88 occupation codes, used to split establishment head counts into managers and non-managers

definition.value: Head count (Columns (1) and (3)) or efficiency units (Column (2)) of non-managers employed at establishment i, entering the Cobb-Douglas final-good technology Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta of Eq. (5).

outcome.label: 𝑌𝑖𝑗 — final-good output of establishment i located in j

definition.value: Output of the final good produced by establishment i with the Cobb-Douglas technology Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta of Eq. (5); alpha and beta are recovered from the jointly estimated system of relative labor demand equations (21) and (22) rather than from an output regression.

units.value: Cobb-Douglas output elasticity of production workers in the final-good technology (a share, between 0 and 1)

estimand.target_population: Establishments in the structural estimation sample: non-HQ establishments of multi-establishment firms paired with their firm's HQ

population.description: Establishments used in the structural estimation: non-HQ establishments of multi-establishment firms paired with their firm's HQ, 1996-2016 (29,104 observations)
population.selection: Firms in manufacturing, transportation, business services and finance, insurance and real estate; establishments with a reported location, outside sparsely populated islands, with more than 2 employees and appearing in more than one year; firms with at least 3 workers and fewer than 100 establishments; workers aged 15-80 with hourly wages between 50 and 5,500 DKK and no flagged wage measurement error; establishments for which at least one manager could be identified (about one third of establishments dropped). When a firm has more than two establishments the firm's largest non-HQ establishment is used.

identification.source_of_variation: Commuting-augmented immigration share-shifters (Eqs. (18)-(19)) as labor supply shocks to relative wages, combined with variation in the distance between establishments and their HQ and in its effect over time, which identifies the distance elasticity of communication costs.
identification.instrument: 𝐼𝑆𝐹 𝐿𝑘 − 𝐼𝑆𝐹 𝐿𝑗 and 𝐼𝑆𝐹 𝑀𝑘 − 𝐼𝑆𝐹 𝑀𝑗 (relative commuting-augmented immigration shocks for workers and for managers, HQ municipality k versus establishment municipality j), entered through the labor supply Eqs. (20) estimated jointly with the system

key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form of technology: final-good production is Cobb-Douglas in production workers and a managerial bundle, Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta with alpha, beta in (0,1) and alpha+beta < 1, and the managerial bundle is fixed-proportions, Mcal_ij = min{lambda*mu_j*m_i, theta*tau_j*H}.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. A Cobb-Douglas-bundle version is reported in Online Appendix C.4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument orthogonality in the system: incorporating the first stage dX = b*dZ + de with E[dZ*de] = 0 identifies and consistently estimates the structural parameter vector phi = {alpha, beta, {c_t}} (Cai et al., 2006).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued by reference to Cai et al. (2006); the labor supply Eqs. (20) are estimated jointly with the relative labor demand equations by FGNLS.

rhs: Unobserved time-varying determinants of the establishment's relative labor demand

implies_edges.to: 𝑌𝑖𝑗 — final-good output of establishment i located in j

key_assumptions.assumption: The cost shares gamma_i (share of non-HQ managers in the non-HQ establishment's managerial cost) and omega_h (share of production managers in total HQ managerial cost) are recovered from observed employment and wages and entered at their lagged value to avoid endogeneity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated construction; managers in HQ services are those classified as 'Directors and Chief Executives'. No test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample conditions on establishments for which a manager could be identified, and the HQ's dependent variable uses the firm's largest non-HQ establishment when the firm has more than two establishments.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a requirement of the model (all establishments must have a positive number of workers and managers); no selection correction is attempted.

The observed increase in HQ managerial intensity could instead result from higher managerial productivity at HQ locations, which Column (3) is designed to test

key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form of technology: final-good production is Cobb-Douglas in production workers and a managerial bundle, Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta with alpha, beta in (0,1) and alpha+beta < 1, and the managerial bundle is fixed-proportions, Mcal_ij = min{lambda*mu_j*m_i, theta*tau_j*H}.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. A Cobb-Douglas-bundle version is reported in Online Appendix C.4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument orthogonality in the system: incorporating the first stage dX = b*dZ + de with E[dZ*de] = 0 identifies and consistently estimates the structural parameter vector phi = {alpha, beta, {c_t}} (Cai et al., 2006).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued by reference to Cai et al. (2006); the labor supply Eqs. (20) are estimated jointly with the relative labor demand equations by FGNLS.

population.selection: Firms in manufacturing, transportation, business services and finance, insurance and real estate; establishments with a reported location, outside sparsely populated islands, with more than 2 employees and appearing in more than one year; firms with at least 3 workers and fewer than 100 establishments; workers aged 15-80 with hourly wages between 50 and 5,500 DKK and no flagged wage measurement error; establishments for which at least one manager could be identified (about one third of establishments dropped). key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form of technology: final-good production is Cobb-Douglas in production workers and a managerial bundle, Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta with alpha, beta in (0,1) and alpha+beta < 1, and the managerial bundle is fixed-proportions, Mcal_ij = min{lambda*mu_j*m_i, theta*tau_j*H}.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. A Cobb-Douglas-bundle version is reported in Online Appendix C.4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument orthogonality in the system: incorporating the first stage dX = b*dZ + de with E[dZ*de] = 0 identifies and consistently estimates the structural parameter vector phi = {alpha, beta, {c_t}} (Cai et al., 2006).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued by reference to Cai et al. (2006); the labor supply Eqs. (20) are estimated jointly with the relative labor demand equations by FGNLS.

key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form of technology: final-good production is Cobb-Douglas in production workers and a managerial bundle, Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta with alpha, beta in (0,1) and alpha+beta < 1, and the managerial bundle is fixed-proportions, Mcal_ij = min{lambda*mu_j*m_i, theta*tau_j*H}.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. A Cobb-Douglas-bundle version is reported in Online Appendix C.4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument orthogonality in the system: incorporating the first stage dX = b*dZ + de with E[dZ*de] = 0 identifies and consistently estimates the structural parameter vector phi = {alpha, beta, {c_t}} (Cai et al., 2006).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued by reference to Cai et al. (2006); the labor supply Eqs. (20) are estimated jointly with the relative labor demand equations by FGNLS.

key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form of technology: final-good production is Cobb-Douglas in production workers and a managerial bundle, Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta with alpha, beta in (0,1) and alpha+beta < 1, and the managerial bundle is fixed-proportions, Mcal_ij = min{lambda*mu_j*m_i, theta*tau_j*H}.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. A Cobb-Douglas-bundle version is reported in Online Appendix C.4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued by reference to Cai et al. (2006); the labor supply Eqs. (20) are estimated jointly with the relative labor demand equations by FGNLS.

key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form of technology: final-good production is Cobb-Douglas in production workers and a managerial bundle, Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta with alpha, beta in (0,1) and alpha+beta < 1, and the managerial bundle is fixed-proportions, Mcal_ij = min{lambda*mu_j*m_i, theta*tau_j*H}.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued by reference to Cai et al. (2006); the labor supply Eqs. (20) are estimated jointly with the relative labor demand equations by FGNLS.

population.description: Establishments used in the structural estimation: non-HQ establishments of multi-establishment firms paired with their firm's HQ, 1996-2016 (29,104 observations)
population.selection: Firms in manufacturing, transportation, business services and finance, insurance and real estate; establishments with a reported location, outside sparsely populated islands, with more than 2 employees and appearing in more than one year; firms with at least 3 workers and fewer than 100 establishments; workers aged 15-80 with hourly wages between 50 and 5,500 DKK and no flagged wage measurement error; establishments for which at least one manager could be identified (about one third of establishments dropped). When a firm has more than two establishments the firm's largest non-HQ establishment is used.

identification.source_of_variation: Commuting-augmented immigration share-shifters (Eqs. (18)-(19)) as labor supply shocks to relative wages, combined with variation in the distance between establishments and their HQ and in its effect over time, which identifies the distance elasticity of communication costs.
identification.instrument: 𝐼𝑆𝐹 𝐿𝑘 − 𝐼𝑆𝐹 𝐿𝑗 and 𝐼𝑆𝐹 𝑀𝑘 − 𝐼𝑆𝐹 𝑀𝑗 (relative commuting-augmented immigration shocks for workers and for managers, HQ municipality k versus establishment municipality j), entered through the labor supply Eqs. (20) estimated jointly with the system

key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form of technology: final-good production is Cobb-Douglas in production workers and a managerial bundle, Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta with alpha, beta in (0,1) and alpha+beta < 1, and the managerial bundle is fixed-proportions, Mcal_ij = min{lambda*mu_j*m_i, theta*tau_j*H}.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. A Cobb-Douglas-bundle version is reported in Online Appendix C.4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument orthogonality in the system: incorporating the first stage dX = b*dZ + de with E[dZ*de] = 0 identifies and consistently estimates the structural parameter vector phi = {alpha, beta, {c_t}} (Cai et al., 2006).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued by reference to Cai et al. (2006); the labor supply Eqs. (20) are estimated jointly with the relative labor demand equations by FGNLS.

rhs: Unobserved time-varying determinants of the establishment's relative labor demand

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated construction; managers in HQ services are those classified as 'Directors and Chief Executives'. No test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form of technology: final-good production is Cobb-Douglas in production workers and a managerial bundle, Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta with alpha, beta in (0,1) and alpha+beta < 1, and the managerial bundle is fixed-proportions, Mcal_ij = min{lambda*mu_j*m_i, theta*tau_j*H}.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

population.selection: Firms in manufacturing, transportation, business services and finance, insurance and real estate; establishments with a reported location, outside sparsely populated islands, with more than 2 employees and appearing in more than one year; firms with at least 3 workers and fewer than 100 establishments; workers aged 15-80 with hourly wages between 50 and 5,500 DKK and no flagged wage measurement error; establishments for which at least one manager could be identified (about one third of establishments dropped). key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form of technology: final-good production is Cobb-Douglas in production workers and a managerial bundle, Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta with alpha, beta in (0,1) and alpha+beta < 1, and the managerial bundle is fixed-proportions, Mcal_ij = min{lambda*mu_j*m_i, theta*tau_j*H}.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. A Cobb-Douglas-bundle version is reported in Online Appendix C.4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument orthogonality in the system: incorporating the first stage dX = b*dZ + de with E[dZ*de] = 0 identifies and consistently estimates the structural parameter vector phi = {alpha, beta, {c_t}} (Cai et al., 2006).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued by reference to Cai et al. (2006); the labor supply Eqs. (20) are estimated jointly with the relative labor demand equations by FGNLS.

population.selection: Firms in manufacturing, transportation, business services and finance, insurance and real estate; establishments with a reported location, outside sparsely populated islands, with more than 2 employees and appearing in more than one year; firms with at least 3 workers and fewer than 100 establishments; workers aged 15-80 with hourly wages between 50 and 5,500 DKK and no flagged wage measurement error; establishments for which at least one manager could be identified (about one third of establishments dropped). When a firm has more than two establishments the firm's largest non-HQ establishment is used.

identification.source_of_variation: Commuting-augmented immigration share-shifters (Eqs. (18)-(19)) as labor supply shocks to relative wages, combined with variation in the distance between establishments and their HQ and in its effect over time, which identifies the distance elasticity of communication costs.
identification.instrument: 𝐼𝑆𝐹 𝐿𝑘 − 𝐼𝑆𝐹 𝐿𝑗 and 𝐼𝑆𝐹 𝑀𝑘 − 𝐼𝑆𝐹 𝑀𝑗 (relative commuting-augmented immigration shocks for workers and for managers, HQ municipality k versus establishment municipality j), entered through the labor supply Eqs. (20) estimated jointly with the system

key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form of technology: final-good production is Cobb-Douglas in production workers and a managerial bundle, Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta with alpha, beta in (0,1) and alpha+beta < 1, and the managerial bundle is fixed-proportions, Mcal_ij = min{lambda*mu_j*m_i, theta*tau_j*H}.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. A Cobb-Douglas-bundle version is reported in Online Appendix C.4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument orthogonality in the system: incorporating the first stage dX = b*dZ + de with E[dZ*de] = 0 identifies and consistently estimates the structural parameter vector phi = {alpha, beta, {c_t}} (Cai et al., 2006).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued by reference to Cai et al. (2006); the labor supply Eqs. (20) are estimated jointly with the relative labor demand equations by FGNLS.

rhs: Unobserved time-varying determinants of the establishment's relative labor demand

implies_edges.from: Commuting-augmented immigration shocks (𝐼𝑆𝐹)
implies_edges.to: Communication costs 𝜏𝑗𝑘 between the establishment's location j and its HQ's location k

key_assumptions.assumption: The cost shares gamma_i (share of non-HQ managers in the non-HQ establishment's managerial cost) and omega_h (share of production managers in total HQ managerial cost) are recovered from observed employment and wages and entered at their lagged value to avoid endogeneity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated construction; managers in HQ services are those classified as 'Directors and Chief Executives'. No test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample conditions on establishments for which a manager could be identified, and the HQ's dependent variable uses the firm's largest non-HQ establishment when the firm has more than two establishments.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a requirement of the model (all establishments must have a positive number of workers and managers); no selection correction is attempted.

implies_edges.from: Sample inclusion: establishment with at least one identified manager
implies_edges.to: Communication costs 𝜏𝑗𝑘 between the establishment's location j and its HQ's location k

threats_discussed: Simultaneity bias: observed wages are equilibrium outcomes

The rising distance elasticity may reflect growing information complexity rather than higher communication costs, and may also be driven by transport infrastructure (the Great Belt Bridge, 1998, and the Oresund Bridge, 2000)
The observed increase in HQ managerial intensity could instead result from higher managerial productivity at HQ locations, which Column (3) is designed to test

key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form of technology: final-good production is Cobb-Douglas in production workers and a managerial bundle, Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta with alpha, beta in (0,1) and alpha+beta < 1, and the managerial bundle is fixed-proportions, Mcal_ij = min{lambda*mu_j*m_i, theta*tau_j*H}.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. A Cobb-Douglas-bundle version is reported in Online Appendix C.4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument orthogonality in the system: incorporating the first stage dX = b*dZ + de with E[dZ*de] = 0 identifies and consistently estimates the structural parameter vector phi = {alpha, beta, {c_t}} (Cai et al., 2006).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued by reference to Cai et al. (2006); the labor supply Eqs. (20) are estimated jointly with the relative labor demand equations by FGNLS.

population.selection: Firms in manufacturing, transportation, business services and finance, insurance and real estate; establishments with a reported location, outside sparsely populated islands, with more than 2 employees and appearing in more than one year; firms with at least 3 workers and fewer than 100 establishments; workers aged 15-80 with hourly wages between 50 and 5,500 DKK and no flagged wage measurement error; establishments for which at least one manager could be identified (about one third of establishments dropped). Eq. (2) is estimated for ME firms.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is claimed: the HQ*year (or year) fixed effects of a two-way fixed-effects regression on the 1996-2016 establishment panel, presented as a stylised fact that motivates the model.

key_assumptions.assumption: Establishment and year fixed effects (plus HQ*year fixed effects and commuting area*sector trends) absorb time-invariant establishment heterogeneity and region-sector trends, so the HQ*year coefficients measure differential changes at HQ relative to non-HQ establishments.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated specification of Eq. (2); commuting area*sector trends are included 'to account for unobservable factors that could be driving these changes at the region and sector level'. Robustness: balanced panel (Figure A1b), excluding firms with an establishment outside Denmark (Figure A1c), excluding the commuting area-sector trends (Figure A1d).

key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued by reference to Cai et al. (2006); the labor supply Eqs. (20) are estimated jointly with the relative labor demand equations by FGNLS.

key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form of technology: final-good production is Cobb-Douglas in production workers and a managerial bundle, Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta with alpha, beta in (0,1) and alpha+beta < 1, and the managerial bundle is fixed-proportions, Mcal_ij = min{lambda*mu_j*m_i, theta*tau_j*H}.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued by reference to Cai et al. (2006); the labor supply Eqs. (20) are estimated jointly with the relative labor demand equations by FGNLS.

key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form of technology: final-good production is Cobb-Douglas in production workers and a managerial bundle, Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta with alpha, beta in (0,1) and alpha+beta < 1, and the managerial bundle is fixed-proportions, Mcal_ij = min{lambda*mu_j*m_i, theta*tau_j*H}.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. A Cobb-Douglas-bundle version is reported in Online Appendix C.4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument orthogonality in the system: incorporating the first stage dX = b*dZ + de with E[dZ*de] = 0 identifies and consistently estimates the structural parameter vector phi = {alpha, beta, {c_t}} (Cai et al., 2006).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued by reference to Cai et al. (2006); the labor supply Eqs. (20) are estimated jointly with the relative labor demand equations by FGNLS.

key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form of technology: final-good production is Cobb-Douglas in production workers and a managerial bundle, Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta with alpha, beta in (0,1) and alpha+beta < 1, and the managerial bundle is fixed-proportions, Mcal_ij = min{lambda*mu_j*m_i, theta*tau_j*H}.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. A Cobb-Douglas-bundle version is reported in Online Appendix C.4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument orthogonality in the system: incorporating the first stage dX = b*dZ + de with E[dZ*de] = 0 identifies and consistently estimates the structural parameter vector phi = {alpha, beta, {c_t}} (Cai et al., 2006).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued by reference to Cai et al. (2006); the labor supply Eqs. (20) are estimated jointly with the relative labor demand equations by FGNLS.

key_assumptions.assumption: Functional form of technology: final-good production is Cobb-Douglas in production workers and a managerial bundle, Y_ij = A L_i^alpha Mcal_ij^beta with alpha, beta in (0,1) and alpha+beta < 1, and the managerial bundle is fixed-proportions, Mcal_ij = min{lambda*mu_j*m_i, theta*tau_j*H}.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cobb-Douglas chosen for tractability (a CES bundle makes the firm's non-linear problem analytically intractable); the fixed-proportions managerial bundle is argued to be consistent with the empirical finding that the across-location elasticity of substitution for managers fades with distance, which a Cobb-Douglas or linear bundle would reverse. A Cobb-Douglas-bundle version is reported in Online Appendix C.4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Communication costs depend only on distance to the HQ and a time-varying elasticity: tau_jk = dist_jk^(-c_t); changes over time in the effect of establishment-HQ distance on labor demand are the main identifying variation for c_t.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assumed because the paper has no direct data on communication costs; the rising estimated c_t is read as rising communication costs, and the paper notes other explanations (information complexity, transport infrastructure such as the Great Belt and Oresund bridges) it cannot separate.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument orthogonality in the system: incorporating the first stage dX = b*dZ + de with E[dZ*de] = 0 identifies and consistently estimates the structural parameter vector phi = {alpha, beta, {c_t}} (Cai et al., 2006).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued by reference to Cai et al. (2006); the labor supply Eqs. (20) are estimated jointly with the relative labor demand equations by FGNLS.

population.description: Establishments used in the structural estimation: non-HQ establishments of multi-establishment firms paired with their firm's HQ, 1996-2016 (29,104 observations)
population.selection: Firms in manufacturing, transportation, business services and finance, insurance and real estate; establishments with a reported location, outside sparsely populated islands, with more than 2 employees and appearing in more than one year; firms with at least 3 workers and fewer than 100 establishments; workers aged 15-80 with hourly wages between 50 and 5,500 DKK and no flagged wage measurement error; establishments for which at least one manager could be identified (about one third of establishments dropped).
